processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Ingots with nominal composition Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%) produced by melting high-purity (>99.9%) raw materials in a vacuum induction furnace under argon.
Hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm.
Plates cut into 10 × 5 × 2 mm3 samples using electrical discharge machining for Vickers hardness measurements and microstructure characterizations.
Solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under argon, followed by oil quenching (parent process proc_st-1100c-10min-oq).
Aged at 575 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching. This is the terminal state of process proc_aging-575c-1h.

structures.overall_structure: Solution-treated 19Al alloy is single-phase α (BCC); the EBSD phase map is uniformly red (α), with a fine equiaxed multi-coloured grain structure. This is the as-solutionized parent state on which aging at 575 °C/1 h is performed.
α (BCC) matrix with a well-developed network of β-Mn decorating the α grain boundaries; only a small amount of β-Mn had formed after 1 h at 575 °C, and the α matrix remained largely untransformed.

interfaces.phase_evolution: α → α + β-Mn: during aging, β-Mn nucleates and grows along α grain boundaries; for the 19Al alloy the α → β-Mn transformation is slow (only a small amount of β-Mn along grain boundaries after 1 h at 575 °C, and untransformed α still observed at 3 h; full transformation requires 10 h at 550 °C).
interfaces.interface_notes: Increase in Al content slowed the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn; at 575 °C the 19Al alloy formed β-Mn only along α grain boundaries, whereas β-Mn also formed within α grains in the 17Al alloy.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Vickers microhardness; load 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample measured 5 times and averaged

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: load 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample measured 5 times and averaged
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the Vickers hardness of the aged 19Al alloy
characterization_methods.key_findings: The 19Al alloy aged at 575 °C for 1 h had a Vickers hardness of 458.7 ± 11.5 HV (Table 4).

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: ZEISS Sigma 300 SEM operated at 5 kV; electrolytically polished using 10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: SE imaging of 19Al samples after different aging treatments (Fig. 9)
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify the precipitation of secondary phases such as α-Mn and β-Mn phases in the aged samples
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 19Al alloy aged at 575 °C for 1 h, an α matrix with a well-developed grain-boundary network of β-Mn was observed.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: GeminiSEM 300 SEM; scanning step size 1.5 μm (low magnification) and 0.05 μm (high magnification)
characterization_methods.purpose: Determine phase constitution and orientation of the solution-treated alloys
characterization_methods.key_findings: The solution-treated 19Al alloy is single-phase α (BCC) with a fine equiaxed multi-coloured grain structure (Fig. 3c).

unmapped_findings: Solution-treated (parent-state) 19Al alloy baseline Vickers hardness is 263.8 ± 1.1 HV (Table 4); aging at 575 °C for 1 h raised the hardness to 458.7 ± 11.5 HV.

Increasing Al content slowed the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn: after 1 h at 575 °C, β-Mn in the 19Al alloy could only be observed along α grain boundaries (and untransformed α was still present even at 3 h), whereas β-Mn in the 17Al alloy also formed within α grains.
For the 19Al alloy, the α → β-Mn transformation was only completed after 10 h at 550 °C, and the optimal aging temperature range for ultra-high hardness is mainly 575–625 °C.
The density of the 19Al alloy measured by the Archimedes method is 6.66 g·cm-3.

Al content of β-Mn in the hardest 19Al sample is 17.5 at.% (SEM-EDS), and the increase in Al slightly enhanced the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn via solid-solution strengthening (general to the alloy series, reported from the hardest samples, not from the 575 °C/1 h condition).
